editor_spans.body: The full text of the Motherwell speech fills in something the advance briefing left out. In my last piece I argued that the 'offer' to Holyrood was mostly a challenge, because Westminster has no power over Scottish local government and can only shame Edinburgh about it. The speech partly answers that. Alongside the talk of 'deep devolution' are two things the UK government really does control: employment support run by the DWP, and innovation and enterprise funding. These are now offered for Scotland to shape. Employment support is the more serious offer, because it is a reserved power that Westminster can give away. Holyrood already runs some employability programmes under the 2016 settlement, so the test is whether money and decisions about benefits come with it, or whether it just means running a UK programme locally.

Watch where the 'Easterhouse principle' sits in the speech. The warm language about 'names not numbers' and an estate project that bought interview clothes and paid bus fares comes right next to 'I won't have a country where we get comfortable with the idea of kids in their 20s just being there on benefits', and next to the Alan Milburn review. Milburn is associated with welfare reform. The Easterhouse model may well be the right way to run employment support. But giving it to Holyrood also hands the Scottish Government a share of a welfare-to-work agenda whose tougher side is being designed in London. If Edinburgh accepts, it takes ownership of the results, including the unpopular ones.

The story of deindustrialisation in the speech is incomplete. It says Ravenscraig and the Leigh pits were shut 'by people hundreds of miles away' who never lived with the results. That is true, but it leaves out who those people were: governments, and the nationalised and privatised industries they shaped, working from a Treasury view that treated a closure as a line in the accounts rather than the loss of a community. The speech's answers are local procurement, its Alexander Dennis buses being the example, and regional control. Neither touches that underlying cause. A Prime Minister who means 'never again' would need to change how the centre counts the cost of closures, not only pass more of the clean-up to the places left behind.
